sources.title: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee (Q377881), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-05): English label 'Bankim Chandra Chatterjee', description 'Bengali writer, poet and journalist (1838-1894)', Korean label 반킴 찬드라 차토파디아야, birth 1838-06-26 and death 1894-04-08. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh), 'Chattopadhyay, Bankimchandra' by Sirajul Islam, read in full. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: writer, journalist and government officer; one of the first BA batch of Calcutta University; deputy magistrate and deputy collector, honoured Rai Bahadur 1891 and CIE 1894, but 'made a place for himself in history not as an executive officer but as a writer'; first celebrated novels Durgeshnandini (1865) and Kapalkundala (1866) written while posted at Baruipur; all fourteen novels published by 1887; his place in Bengali literature 'rests on his contribution to the growth of Bangla fiction and Bangla prose', surpassing his peers in characterisation, description and refining prose; his periodical Bangadarshan (1872-76) 'created a generation of writers' and set a new critical style, though it lasted only four years. Modern scholarly reference with a CRITICAL voice: it judges his later turn to Hindu-revivalist writing, the historical novels and his view of Hindu-Muslim history harshly, and says his literary personality dimmed in later years until overtaken by Tagore and Nazrul. Its political and nationalist material is context only and is not scored.

EBSCO Research Starters, 'Bankim Chandra Chatterji' by Jack Ewing (2024), read in full. A modern reference biography: educated at Hooghly and Presidency College and an early Calcutta University graduate; deputy magistrate in the Indian Civil Service from 1858 to 1891; first novel in English (Rajmohan's Wife), then Durgeshnandini (1865) and Kapalkundala (1866); founded the monthly Bangadarshan in 1872, 'determined to be a positive force in stimulating the intellect of the Bengali people', which carried his stories, humorous sketches, historical essays, religious discourses, criticism and book reviews and serialised Vishavriksha from 1873; alternated essays, humorous sketches and historical or romance fiction; credited with helping establish prose as a viable literary vehicle in Bengali. It also says he was transferred often for failing to show proper respect to his British superiors (single unsourced line, not scored). Independent of the other readings in its details but a short summary.

Romesh Chunder Dutt, 'The Literature of Bengal' (revised edition with portraits; Calcutta: Thacker Spink, and London: Constable, 1895), chapter XIX 'Bankim Chandra Chatterjea and his Novels' and its author's footnote (Internet Archive scan from the University of California Libraries, OCR text read: pages 221 to 235 and the portrait plate). A contemporary Bengali scholar and civil servant, writing a year after Bankim's death: calls him in prose what Madhu Sudan is in verse, 'the founder of a new style'; says Durgeshnandini 'taken by surprise' the literary world and that 'nothing so bold and original had been attempted in Bengali prose'; records that early critics condemned him as a denationalised imitator of European models; describes the Banga Darsan under his editorship as the most popular and ablest journal of the day, with younger writers contributing and profiting from his advice; mentions his novels, humorous tales, essays and a book on Krishna that surprised orthodox readers; and the author's own footnote on how Bankim in 1872 urged him to write in Bengali. Admiring and personal (Dutt was a younger acquaintance and beneficiary), so used with caution.

Sri Aurobindo, 'Bankim Chandra Chatterji' (seven essays written in 1894 for the Indu Prakash, Bombay; Early Cultural Writings, Complete Works vol. 1, Sri Aurobindo Ashram Trust, 2003; Internet Archive scan, OCR text read: sections on his youth, official career, versatility and literary history). A near-contemporary admiring appreciation by a 22-year-old: calls him 'creator and king of Bengali prose', describes his early facility in study and a passion for Sanskrit that fed his new prose, his official postings and a vigorous record against indigo planters and river pirates at Khulna (told in heroic terms, no documents cited), his versatility and the small output of 'ten novels, two critical works on religion and some scattered literature' reckoned by him 'pure gold', first novel written in English then abandoned for Bengali, Durgeshnandini as 'the first-born child of the New Prose', and his editing of the Bangadarshan. Hagiographic in tone and written by a later nationalist leader; used only for episodes that other sources also record. The later 1907 political essay 'Rishi Bankim Chandra' was not used.

Rabindranath Tagore, 'My Reminiscences' (English translation, New York: Macmillan, 1917; Internet Archive scan, OCR text read: the chapter 'Bankim Chandra', the passage on the Bangadarshan serial, and the notes on the Evening Songs and the Academy). A younger fellow writer's account: the Bengali reading public took the serialised Bangadarshan 'by storm' (Chandrasekhar, Vishavriksha); Bankim at a graduates' reunion hurrying from the room when a pandit recited a vulgar verse; Bankim wearing Tagore's Evening Songs garland and praising the book to Ramesh Chandra Dutt; Bankim closing his editorship of the Bangadarshan and starting the monthly Prachar for religious discussions; and a period of public controversy between the two, ended by a letter from Bankim that Tagore says showed 'consummate generosity' (the letter itself is lost). A memoir by a writer who knew him and later became famous himself, so partly self-report about Tagore and partly an independent observation of Bankim; Bankim's role in the Academy was noted as lukewarm.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_bankim_dutt1895, src_bankim_banglapedia, src_bankim_ebsco, src_bankim_aurobindo | 1865-1887 | contemporary scholar, modern encyclopedia, reference biography, admiring appreciation] Dutt (1895) calls him 'the founder of a new style' and says nothing so bold and original had been tried in Bengali prose, and records that early critics dismissed him as an imitator of European models; Banglapedia says earlier Bengali fiction was largely didactic translation and that he surpassed his peers in characterisation, description and the refining of prose; EBSCO says his novels helped create a school of fiction. The modern encyclopedia and the contemporary critic converge, but all are retrospective critical judgements and the form borrows openly from Scott. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 78 / 0.62 to 76 / 0.58 because Dutt and Aurobindo are admiring 1890s voices and the EBSCO summary repeats the same view without its own argument.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_bankim_banglapedia, src_bankim_dutt1895, src_bankim_ebsco, src_bankim_tagore | 1872-1876 | modern encyclopedia, contemporary scholar, reference biography, fellow writer] In 1872, while a serving deputy magistrate, he started the monthly Bangadarshan and edited it; Banglapedia says he wanted it to be a platform for objective criticism on the model of European journals and that it created a generation of writers, EBSCO says he set it up to stimulate the intellect of the Bengali people, Dutt says it became the most popular and ablest journal of its day, and Tagore records the reading public waiting on each serial instalment. The initiative is documented by four separate sources; the weaker part is how far his stated aims were met, since the journal ran only four years.

discipline.rationale: [src_bankim_banglapedia, src_bankim_ebsco, src_bankim_dutt1895, src_bankim_aurobindo | 1858-1891 | modern encyclopedia, reference biography, contemporary scholar, admiring appreciation] He served as a deputy magistrate and deputy collector from 1858 until he retired in 1891 and was praised for doing the job exceedingly well (Banglapedia), while publishing fourteen novels by 1887 plus essays and religious writing; Dutt says literary ambition was his ruling passion and the reading world feasted on his unceasing productions for a generation. The documented fact is sustained output beside a full-time career; the consistency of his working habits is inferred from the output, not described in a source, and the strongest praise of his labour is Aurobindo's.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_bankim_ebsco, src_bankim_dutt1895, src_bankim_banglapedia | 1865-1887 | reference biography, contemporary scholar, modern encyclopedia] EBSCO lists his stories, humorous sketches, historical essays, religious discourses, literary criticism and book reviews in the Bangadarshan and says he alternated essays, humorous sketches and historical, romance or adventure fiction; Dutt names the social, historical and critical essays and the book on Krishna alongside the novels; Banglapedia names the religious monographs. The range across fiction, satire, criticism, editing and religious exegesis is well documented, but it is range within writing and publishing rather than across unrelated fields.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_bankim_dutt1895, src_bankim_banglapedia | 1865-1884 | contemporary scholar, modern encyclopedia] Dutt records that critics and disappointed writers condemned his first novels as the work of a denationalised imitator and that he carried on, and that his book on Krishna argued, to the perplexity of orthodox readers, that the stories of the god's amours were later fabrications; Banglapedia, however, judges that in his later writing he overlooked the real history of Hindu-Muslim relations in Bengal. Taking an unpopular line on tradition is documented, but the quality of the reasoning is disputed by the modern source, so the impact is dual-edged and confidence stays below 0.5. His nationalist slogans and political reception are not scored.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_bankim_ebsco, src_bankim_dutt1895, src_bankim_banglapedia | 1872-1880s | reference biography, contemporary scholar, modern encyclopedia] EBSCO says he was determined to be a positive force in stimulating the intellect of the Bengali people; Dutt, in a footnote, recalls that in 1872 he urged a younger Bengali official-writer to write in Bengali and shows 'zeal for his country's literature'; Banglapedia credits Bangadarshan with raising a generation of writers. The aim is documented in outline but largely through admiring or summary sources and one beneficiary's anecdote. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 68 / 0.52 to 64 / 0.46 because the motive is attributed mainly by admiring retrospective accounts and a single anecdote told by the person he mentored.

portrait.source: Portrait plate 'Bankim Chandra Chatterjea.' facing page 221 of Romesh Chunder Dutt, The Literature of Bengal, revised edition with portraits (Calcutta: Thacker Spink; London: Constable, 1895), from the University of California Libraries scan on the Internet Archive (item literatureofbeng00duttrich). The plate is a printed engraving by an unnamed engraver (illegible monogram) after an unnamed original, probably a photograph made in his lifetime; it is shown as a printed likeness copy, not as a documented sitting. The printed caption on the plate leaf names him. The file is the plate crop at 1626 x 2467 downscaled to 791 x 1200 with no upscaling.
